Market Note 01 · The learning series

Why bond prices fall when yields rise

The coupon can stay the same while the price and the return available to a new buyer change.

3-minute read · Evergreen educational draft

The payments stay fixed; the price does not

A fixed-rate bond promises specified payments. Its market price changes as buyers change the return they require. If comparable yields rise, the same promised dollars become less attractive at yesterday’s price. A lower price gives a new buyer a higher yield. This is the inverse price–yield relationship described by Investor.gov / SEC.

Follow one bond through three yields

Consider an illustrative bond with $100 face value, a fixed 4% annual coupon and exactly three years remaining. We value it immediately after a coupon payment, so no accrued interest is owed. The remaining payments are $4 in one year, $4 in two years and $104 in three years.

Discounting means translating a future payment into today’s money using the return required for waiting. Using one annual yield, y, our simplified price is:

P = 4/(1+y) + 4/(1+y)² + 104/(1+y)³

That is also the three $4 coupons, discounted separately, plus the discounted $100 repayment. The table holds every payment and date constant; only the required yield changes. These are calculated examples, not market quotes.

Illustrative bond prices, immediately after a coupon payment
Annual YTMPrice per $100 faceCurrent yield
2%$105.773.78%
4%$100.004.00%
6%$94.654.23%

Four terms that answer different questions

The coupon rate sets the payment: 4% of $100, or $4 each year. It stays fixed here. Current yield divides that $4 by today’s price. At $94.65 it is approximately 4.23%; it ignores the gain from eventually receiving $100.

Yield to maturity, or YTM, is the annual discount rate that matches all remaining promised payments to the purchase price. In our last row it is 6%, incorporating both coupons and repayment at face value. Realised total return is the actual outcome, including income, reinvestment and the eventual sale or repayment. Costs and taxes also matter. Converting YTM into a realised compound return requires the payments to arrive and coupons to be reinvested at that rate. It is not a guaranteed result. FINRA explains these distinctions.

Where the Fed fits—and where it does not

The Fed targets an overnight interest rate between banks. A three-year bond’s market yield is a different rate. Longer yields reflect expectations for future policy and the economy, as the Federal Reserve explains. A widely anticipated hike may already be reflected in bond prices before the announcement.

A hike therefore does not guarantee that every market yield rises that day. Different maturities can move differently along the yield curve, which plots yields against time to maturity. Our one-yield example explains a bond’s pricing arithmetic; it does not predict that curve’s next move.

When reading a headline, ask: did the policy rate change, did this bond’s market yield change, or did its coupon change? Those are three different statements.

See the calculation

Price = 4/(1+y) + 4/(1+y)² + 104/(1+y)³, where y is the annual yield as a decimal. At 2%, the price is $105.77; at 4%, $100.00; at 6%, $94.65.
